A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same episodic risk-sensitive linear quadratic control work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated theoretical material.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original simulations of both proposed algorithms on a synthetic LEQR system, averaging regret over 30 independent runs.

after.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D report original simulations on three LEQR systems, including risk-parameter and horizon comparisons, using 150 independent runs.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1 and 2 retain the same least-squares estimators, Riccati-based controllers, update schedules, and exploration-noise rule. The explicit anytime restart schedule elaborates the previously mentioned doubling trick; the revised simulation parameters do not establish a new method.

E1.justification: The single synthetic positive-definite system in v1 is replaced by three systems: a model sourced from Dean et al. (2020), a nonsymmetric random system, and a flying-robot model sourced from Tsiamis et al. (2020). Section 5 and Appendix D substantially broaden the evaluated dynamics and application coverage.

E2.justification: V1 plots the proposed algorithms alongside reference growth curves. V2 adds evaluated risk-neutral comparators in the risk-parameter panels of Figures 1–3; Section 5 identifies Algorithm 1 with gamma = 0 as corresponding to Basei et al. (2022). The other gamma settings are sensitivity variants.

E3.justification: The experimental design is substantially replaced. V1 uses T = 10 and gamma = 0.02; v2 introduces risk-misspecification comparisons around a true gamma of 0.1 and horizon sweeps over T = 3, 4, 5. The reported initial epoch size changes from 800 to 500 and regularization from 0.1 to 0.8, alongside revised initialization and system configurations.

E4.justification: V1 only illustrates regret growth for the two algorithms. V2 adds systematic tests of misspecified risk aversion, including risk-neutral operation, and sensitivity to episode horizon for both algorithms across all three systems. These analyses appear in Figure 1 and Appendix D, Figures 2–3.

E5.justification: V1 averages 30 independent runs and explicitly omits plotted confidence intervals because they are narrow. V2 reports 150 independent runs and specifies and displays 95% confidence intervals for the principal regret curves. This refines replication and uncertainty reporting for the replacement experiments.

E6.justification: The original two simulation curves are replaced by results for three systems and multiple parameter settings. Newly reported findings include higher finite-sample regret for Algorithm 1 than Algorithm 2 in System 1, increased eventual regret under risk misspecification, and greater regret with longer horizons. These are results under new conditions, not same-setting improvements over v1.

T1.justification: The main assumptions, Theorems 1–2, Riccati equations, and appendix proofs are unchanged in substance. V1 Appendix A.4.1 becomes v2 Appendix C with the same parameter-dependence derivations; the added explanation connecting the two theorems does not supply a new formal result.

C1.justification: The central logarithmic and square-root regret contributions remain. However, v2 removes the introduction's separate novelty claim that square-root regret was previously unavailable even for risk-neutral episodic LQR, focusing the contribution statement on risk-sensitive LEQR.

C2.justification: V2 attributes Algorithm 1's poorer finite-sample performance to infrequent parameter updates and inaccurate initial estimates, and discusses the consequences of misspecified risk aversion. Its conclusion also identifies perturbation analysis of generalized algebraic Riccati equations as an obstacle to extending the results to the non-episodic setting.

D1.justification: V2 specifies uniform sampling for the new random system and initial estimates, identifies source sections and cost-matrix modifications for the borrowed systems, and makes the anytime restart schedule explicit. Hardware information is retained, and neither version provides a code release.

R1.justification: V2 adds focused positioning relative to H-infinity adaptive control, financial liquidation applications, and persistence of excitation, with corresponding citations. It also adds benchmark sources and removes Tsiamis et al. (2023). The principal relationship to Basei et al. and risk-sensitive reinforcement learning remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and simulation discussion receive localized rewrites, numbered remarks are consolidated into prose, and risk-aversion and anytime-operation explanations expand. The parameter-dependence discussion moves to Appendix C and simulation Appendix D is added, while the main section sequence and proof organization remain.

P2.justification: V1's two-panel simulation display is replaced by three six-panel figures covering regret, risk parameters, and horizons. V2 introduces confidence-interval curves and multi-setting legends, while removing the original reference-rate overlays and log-log presentation. This substantially revises the empirical displays.

improvement.justification: Section 5 and Appendix D provide broader empirical illustrations, visible uncertainty, and useful diagnostics of risk misspecification and horizon dependence. Explaining Algorithm 1's poorer finite-sample performance also improves practical interpretation. These strengthen validation and exposition, while the paper's central theoretical guarantees and proofs remain unchanged.
